title: Earning enrollment
content:
The single most important factor in learning is whether the student is actively engaged in the process.

Eyes bright, hands up, curious and eager for the insight on the other side.

Ask any teacher–students like this are a delight.

The same is true for the work of professionals–from doctors to cashiers. Wanting to be there, open to interaction, eager for change–these are so obvious that we usually overlook them.

In fact, the real work of anyone building an institution of learning or an organization that seeks to serve is simple: create the conditions for people to choose to actively participate.

The lazy method is to wait for the self-motivated and take credit for the results when they show up. The hard work is to build the systems and culture that makes it more likely that you’re attracting, motivating and transforming the people who want to go where you can take them.

Everything else is a bonus.

title: Emergent properties
content:
No system stays the way it began, and all systems evolve characteristics that surprise us.

The rise of the automobile system led to roads and gas stations, of course, but also parking lots, drive-through fast food restaurants and drunk driving.

The TV industrial complex was based on the effectiveness of advertising, and the ads that were among the most profitable were for beverages and snack foods, which made those industries ever more efficient and led to convenience foods and also widespread obesity.

And factory farming feeds billions of people. Competitive pressures led to a rise in fertilizer use and a destruction of topsoil, which also dramatically shifts the climate.

Any complex system will soon surprise us with its unanticipated effects.

title: The Fortunes of a Dim Sun
content:
In a classic 1972 paper, astronomers Carl Sagan and George Mullen presented what became known as the Faint Young Sun paradox. Billions of years ago, the sun was a quarter to a third fainter than it is today, and the young Earth should have been completely frozen over. Yet there is geological evidence that there was already liquid water back then. Somehow Earth kept warm, and to this day it’s not entirely clear how it would have done so.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from _Nautilus_.  
To get it in print, **[join by Nov 30](https://nautil.us/hotissue?utm_source=beehiiv&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=issuerelease-issue69-t1-202611&utm_term=free)**.

It turns out that we may have had this problem backward. Recent climate simulations find that Earth may have _needed_ the young sun to be faint for its oceans to form in the first place.

To see why, let’s compare the divergent fates of Venus and Earth. These two worlds formed as next-door neighbors. They grew from rocky material that collided and stuck together. They also had access to the same sources of water.

Our understanding of the origins of Earth’s water has undergone a drastic rethinking in recent years. Scientists have been studying a type of meteorite known as enstatite chondrites, which match our planet’s isotopic composition and may therefore be a sample of the material from which it formed. These meteorites contain far more water than previously thought. That means Earth had water from the start as part of its raw material. And that, in turn, means Venus, though desiccated today, was originally wet, too. Consistent with this, the hydrogen in Venus’s atmosphere is predominantly in the form of its heavy isotope, deuterium. That indicates the planet’s water broke down into the constituent hydrogen and oxygen. Some of the hydrogen was ordinary hydrogen, which was lost to space, and some was deuterium, which, being heavier, stayed behind. In fact, the planet might once have had as much water as Earth.

The difference between Earth and Venus was probably not what they formed from. Rather, it was what came next.

The final phase of planet formation involved a handful of giant impacts between planetary embryos; one of those is thought to have formed the moon. Each impact produced a giant pulse of heat, melting the entire surface of the growing planets. Any surface water was boiled off into a thick steam atmosphere. The question becomes whether that steam could rain out to create oceans.

One key element is rotation. Earth completes one spin in 24 hours. Venus takes 243 days. The planets’ spin rates were first set during their formation, mainly by the angular momentum imparted in the last one or two impacts. Earth’s spin was initially much faster—a day took just four hours—but gradually slowed under the moon’s gravitational pull. Venus’s slow spin is not fully understood. It’s thought to be a combination of several effects, including a giant impact that hit the planet in just the right way, and powerful tides that the sun raised in the planet’s thick atmosphere.

On a slowly rotating planet, the side that faces the sun develops a persistent, thick cloud deck. Being white and puffy, these clouds have a big impact on the climate by reflecting a large fraction of the sun’s energy back into space. Because the clouds are located exactly where the planet is most strongly irradiated, they change the planet’s energy balance. A 2013 paper by climate modelers Jun Yang, Nicolas Cowan, and Dorian Abbot, who were all then at the University of Chicago, showed that the presence of these clouds can allow water to exist on a planet that otherwise seems too close to its star. The effect is fed by a stabilizing feedback loop: If the planet heats up a little, atmospheric convection is strengthened, which thickens the clouds and cools the planet off.

In the parlance of astronomy, this mechanism of cloud formation alters our estimate of where the habitable zone lies—the Goldilocks belt around a star where conditions are neither too hot nor too cold but just right for liquid water to persist on a planet’s surface. Clouds push the inner edge of the habitable zone inward by about a third in distance. In 2016, a study led by Michael Way at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies in New York used a series of climate simulations to argue that, because Venus rotates slowly, it could have built a cooling cloud deck on its dayside and been habitable for billions of years.

But Way and colleagues assumed that Venus started with oceans. In 2021, a study led by planetary astronomer Martin Turbet, now at the Institut Pierre-Simon Laplace in Paris, attacked the problem from the other side, asking whether oceans could ever have condensed out of Venus’s early, steam-dominated atmosphere. Their answer was no. Instead of building up on the dayside, where they would have cooled the planet, the clouds gathered on the night side. They blocked infrared cooling so efficiently and trapped so much heat that they kept the planet too hot for rain to ever reach the surface. Put simply, dayside clouds are parasols, but nightside clouds are patio heaters, and early Venus was dominated by the latter.

Turbet and colleagues showed that forming an ocean requires sunlight to be subdued. The condensation limit is at about 95 percent of our current sunlight intensity. The young Earth got 70 to 75 percent as much, so its oceans were able to condense. The young Venus got about 135 percent, so it stayed a steam world. Had the young sun been as bright as today’s, Earth would have met the same fate.

COULD IT RAIN?: Venus, in this NASA photo, is surrounded by sulfuric acid clouds. Astronomers have asked whether oceans could ever have condensed out of the planet’s early, steam-dominated atmosphere. _Credit: NASA / JPL_

Today, Venus is shrouded in clouds, but they are a different beast. They are made of sulfuric acid, not water, and they float in a dry, carbon dioxide atmosphere. They reflect about three-quarters of incoming sunlight, so much that Venus actually absorbs less solar energy than Earth does. Yet its surface is a scorching 860 degrees Fahrenheit. The culprit is the greenhouse effect, so that the little sunlight that gets through to the surface is trapped as heat.

Mars was the opposite case. Being farther from the sun, it was cooler, and oceans could have rained out from a steam atmosphere. But keeping the water liquid was a problem. We see plenty of geologic evidence that early Mars had liquid water, but we don’t know how long it persisted. The planet may have had a much thicker atmosphere able to maintain liquid water, or the liquid water may have been only intermittent—after meteor impacts provided temporary pulses of heat. In either case, with its small mass, Mars cooled off quickly and lost its magnetic field, leaving its atmosphere exposed to being stripped away by charged particles streaming out from the sun.

In a 2023 follow-up paper, Turbet and colleagues mapped out the “water condensation zone,” the sub-domain of the habitable zone inside which a planet could rain out an ocean from its atmosphere and then keep that ocean. The location of such a zone depends on the type of star. Red dwarf stars, which are smaller than the sun and highly numerous in the galaxy, are extra bright in youth and then barely brighten afterward. Planets around those stars can’t catch a break. As a result, for several planets that are currently considered prime habitable-zone targets, the question isn’t whether they could keep an ocean, but whether they ever had one.

Looking to the future, Earth is in trouble. The brightening trend that Sagan and Mullen talked about is continuing. The reason has to do with how stars generate energy via nuclear fusion. Stars such as the sun are powered by the proton-proton chain of reactions, which uses four hydrogen atoms to produce a single helium atom. This releases energy that percolates through the star and eventually emerges as starlight. As fusion takes place, the number of particles goes down. This causes the gas pressure to decrease and the core to become more compressed and hotter. This, in turn, increases the rate of atomic encounters and of nuclear fusion, and the brightness of the sun thereby increases. This effect is too slow to be visible on human timescales, but accumulates over the eons.

That means the habitable zone is slowly marching outward, to wider orbits. Its inner edge is now only slightly inside Earth’s orbit, and it is inexorably approaching. About a billion years from now, Earth will join Venus in the too-hot region of our solar system.

Could Earth develop more clouds to reduce incoming solar radiation? A little, perhaps. Climate models disagree on how Earth’s clouds will respond to a brighter sun. But a fast-spinning planet such as ours can’t build a permanent parasol as many slow rotators can. In a 2014 paper, Yang and collaborators showed that the location of the inner edge of the habitable zone depends strongly on a planet’s spin rate. On a fast rotator, the Coriolis force—the same effect that accounts for the rotation of a hurricane—breaks up the dayside cloud deck and shreds the parasol.

Earth is not immediately doomed. The carbonate-silicate cycle that regulates the atmosphere over geologic time will respond by drawing more carbon dioxide down into the seafloor. This will buy us time. But once carbon dioxide drops too low for photosynthesis—somewhere around a billion years from now—the geologic thermostat can’t help anymore. The amount of water in the atmosphere will increase and, since water is itself a strong greenhouse gas, generate feedback in which increasing water content leads to more heating, which increases the water content, and so on, until the oceans boil away. Not a rosy future.

Earth needed a dim sun to make its oceans and a greenhouse to keep them liquid. To keep them a billion years from now, it will need shade, and it can’t grow its own. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Oceans and Forests Have Absorbed Roughly Half Our Carbon Emissions for Decades, Slowing Climate Change. But Can They Keep It Up?
content:
Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere [by burning fossil fuels](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-3211-2026), raising global temperatures in the process.

Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.

The world’s [oceans have absorbed 35%](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544) of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.

The oceans absorb a large amount of humanity’s carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels. That amount has been increasing, but new research suggests the increase will slow in the coming decades. _Credit: Joachim Lesne/Unsplash_

The importance of these two enormous [natural carbon sinks](https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/carbon-sources-and-sinks/) cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, [fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-11/) around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.

If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their [remaining carbon budgets](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-023-01848-5) – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.

But what if those carbon sinks change?

Earth’s forests take in large amounts of carbon dioxide. But they can also become carbon sources, especially if the climate continues to change. _Credit: Crystal Mirallegro/Unsplash_

We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an [alternative method for measuring](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544) these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that [expansion might begin to slow down](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544), leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.

**The Fiendishly Difficult Task of Measuring Carbon Sinks**

Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.

[Computer models](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-9-1937-2016) can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. [Satellites](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021RG000736) can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.

The 10-year running averages for the two global carbon sinks – land and ocean – show the ocean absorbing much more, but that increase in how much it absorbs is slowing. The land sink does not show an increasing trend in recent decades. _Credit: Figure adapted from Morgan et al., Science, 2026; atmospheric CO2 data from NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory; atmospheric O2 data from Scripps Institution of Oceanography_

As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.

Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used [high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-095975-7.00420-4) (O₂), combined with [atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements](https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/global.html), to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks take up carbon dioxide.

This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.

This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.

**What We Found**

When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.

In contrast to most [computer model simulations](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00456-3), we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than [predicted by most models](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GB007780), and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.

The 10-year running averages for the two global carbon sinks – land and ocean – show the ocean absorbing much more, but that increase in how much it absorbs is slowing. The land sink does not show an increasing trend in recent decades. _Credit:_ _Adapted from Morgan et al., Science, 2026, supplementary materials_

**Where Is the Climate Headed?**

If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.

For example, warmer waters are [not able to hold as much gas](https://news.wisc.edu/climate-change-reducing-oceans-carbon-dioxide-uptake/), such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at [mixing into the deep ocean](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/oceans-carbon-balance/), which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years.

Warmer waters can’t hold as much carbon dioxide or mix as well with lower ocean layers. _Credit: Cristian Palmer/Unsplash_

The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.

**Carbon Cycle Models Need to Improve**

For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.

Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dXBzFNEwoj8)

**Looking Ahead**

We believe our study improves [understanding of global carbon sinks](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544) and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.

The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. [Calibrating the measurements](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-0889.2006.00196.x) is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they [expel some oxygen into the atmosphere](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-018-0152-2). We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.

Policymakers and the public [need answers faster](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-19-0017.1). We believe the solution involves both [improving the atmospheric oxygen approach](https://amt.copernicus.org/articles/16/387/2023/) and using other independent approaches: measurements of [carbon](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2022.0063) and [oxygen](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024jh000272) in the oceans, [computer](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023ms003840)[models](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021gb007177) and [satellites](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.earscirev.2024.104682) are all essential. Combining these approaches will lead to more robust understanding of the carbon cycle and climate change, and better knowledge of where these valuable carbon sinks and the global climate are headed. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Why Are These Polar Bears Thriving?
content:
It was my turn to watch for polar bears, though I wasn’t entirely sure what watching for one on a hot beach in summer was supposed to look like. Around me, on a tiny island in James Bay in Quebec, Canada, the field team moved with practiced efficiency, unspooling barbed wire and setting up a camera trap. I found an elevated spot on the warm ground, and periodically glanced over my shoulder at the dense, low-slung pine forest behind us. Arctic terns darted like paper planes above our heads. Beluga whales crested against the horizon.

“Don’t worry, the bears are probably asleep right now,” Harry Erless, squinting into the midday sun, assured me. Erless, gregarious as he is knowledgeable, is an experienced ranger and trapper of the Cree Nation of Waskaganish, an Indigenous community on the southeast shore of James Bay.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from _Nautilus_.  
To get it in print, **[join by Nov 30](https://nautil.us/hotissue?utm_source=beehiiv&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=issuerelease-issue69-t1-202611&utm_term=free)**.

The scene felt entirely upside-down, and not just because I have never seen a polar bear in the wild. I had trouble picturing one here in the first place. This area, known as the Eeyou Marine Region, lies at the southernmost fringe of the polar bears’ global range, at roughly the same latitude as London, England. By every standard ecological narrative, polar bears should be disappearing from here. With warming global temperatures, the Eeyou Marine Region is seeing a trend toward longer summers and earlier sea ice breakup in the bay. Yet what brought me here was news of a paradox: The polar bears appear to be thriving.

In July 2026, I traveled to Waskaganish to learn more about this apparent contradiction. Since 2021, local Cree trappers and wildlife scientists have been building a partnership that pairs traditional Indigenous knowledge with Western field science. Their project offers a hopeful new framework for conservation in a rapidly changing Arctic.

“Our main objective with this work is to prevent conflict,” Sanford Diamond, son of a former chief of the Cree Nation of Waskaganish, told me shortly before we set out. From the Cree perspective, the true peril of a warming bay is that polar bears, unable to hunt on ice, are forced to spend more time on shore and come into increasing contact with coastal communities.

“Our people, we don’t harvest something when we don’t eat it. And we don’t eat the polar bear,” Diamond told me. But defense-of-life kills become unavoidable when a bear threatens human safety or property. The risk is highest during the annual spring goose hunt, when hunters and bears converge on the islands near the mainland.

For the scientists, the central question is: What makes this southernmost population of polar bears appear so resilient?

“It seems like there’s something special about James Bay that’s allowing bears to persist,” said Alexandra Langwieder, a doctoral researcher at McGill University who leads the scientific side of the project. Despite the diminishing ice, the bay and its small islands may offer the bears easy posts to prey on seals. They could also be feeding on terrestrial mammals like beavers and scavenging on carcasses of larger animals like caribou and belugas.

**BEAR WATCH:** Bernard Diamond, a member of the Cree Trappers Association, surveys the shore on Carey Island in James Bay, Quebec, Canada. _Credit: Elena Kazamia_

I spent a whole day zipping around the bay with the project’s field team, deploying polar bear monitoring stations scattered across 250 miles of the Eeyou Marine Region. We crisscrossed the east side of the bay in two open fiberglass fishing boats, the sound of our engines bouncing across the still water. It was a stunning clear day, with deep-blue skies and the shallow bay lying open like a dish.

I joined Eeyou Marine Region Wildlife Board scientist Manon Sorais in the boat captained by Erless, who navigated the vast expanse seamlessly by sight, reading water currents and subtle shifts in wind. His childhood friend and fellow trapper Bernard Diamond followed closely in the second boat with Sorais’ colleague, Félix Boulanger.

I watched as Bernard Diamond collected driftwood while Erless unspooled a coil of barbed wire. Working in a 10-foot triangle, he strung the wire hip-high across three steel T-posts pounded into the tundra substrate. In the center, Diamond liberally coated the driftwood with a pungent mixture of commercial fish oil and fryer grease, stacking rocks over it so the summer rain wouldn’t wash the scent away. This is to lure the polar bears. A few feet off the perimeter, Sorais and Boulanger hammered a fourth post to mount a motion-activated Reconyx camera inside a steel security box.

Such a design for monitoring polar bears is simple, elegant, and entirely noninvasive. When a curious bear steps into the triangle to sniff the lure, its flank brushes the wire, leaving behind a few strands of fur before it wanders off unharmed. Camera footage helps scientists identify the sex of the bear and provides a quick visual assessment of condition.

For decades, polar bear research meant chasing animals in low-flying helicopters, shooting them with tranquilizer darts, and strapping on radio collars—a practice long opposed by northern Indigenous communities concerned about animal welfare. By contrast, this network of monitoring stations, co-designed by Cree trappers and Langwieder, offers a community-led alternative that respects Indigenous sovereignty while yielding precise scientific data.

The hair snagged by the barbed wire is a gold mine of information. “We chop off the root of the hair to get the genetics, and we use the rest of the shaft for stable isotope analysis,” Langwieder told me. “That represents the diet while the hair is growing.”

This biochemical timeline captures the critical months when bears feed most actively to fatten up for winter or denning. Conventional ecological wisdom holds that bears forced ashore are essentially fasting, losing between 2 and 4.5 pounds of body mass per day without blubber-rich marine prey. By measuring isotope signatures, scientists can address the central paradox of why polar bears in the Eeyou Marine Region appear so healthy despite spending less time on the ice—pinpointing whether they successfully hunted marine mammals during this period or were forced to dine on terrestrial alternatives.

**A BETTER BEAR TRAP:** Manon Sorais, a wildlife management biologist at the Eeyou Marine Region Wildlife Board, adjusts a monitoring-station pole, as Cree trapper Harry Erless and Felix Boulanger, also an Eeyou wildlife management biologist, work closer to the shore. _Credit: Elena Kazamia_

Since the project launched, hair snares and camera traps have cataloged 94 individual bears across the Eeyou Marine Region, with an even split between males and females. Visually, the data reveal a population that is well-fed. Using a standardized five-point fatness index, scientists found that nearly 80 percent of the bears photographed on these islands scored as “average” or “visibly fat.”

“A lot of it is related to fat on key points of the body—the shoulder, the hip, how low the belly is. It’s a qualitative measure of condition,” Langwieder explained.

However, she cautions against reading too much into this data. While early summer fat stores look promising, they cannot shield bears from the severe late-season depletion that lies ahead.

“It’s not hard to find healthy polar bears at the start of summer almost anywhere,” Langwieder said. The broader Southern Hudson Bay subpopulation of bears (of which the Eeyou Marine Region is one small part) reflects a sobering trend: Driven by an ice-free season that has expanded by up to a month since the 1980s, bear numbers have dropped by 17 percent between 2011 and 2016 alongside a steady, long-term decline in body condition.

What looks more promising, Langwieder said, are field observations in the Eeyou Marine Region of females accompanied by healthy cubs—including rare sightings of triplet litters, a biological luxury usually reserved for regions with prime, stable sea ice. “We see cubs every year—quite a few cubs,” Langwieder said.

At our next mooring, Erless took a moment to smoke a cigarette by the boat, and I hung back with him. He pointed out a deep hollow scooped into the embankment right at the water’s edge. “Do you see this blind?” he asked. “This is a polar bear blind, and you can see where they dug. They wait here for a seal, patiently, and that’s where they hunt.”

Observations like this offer a compelling explanation for why the bear population appears healthy despite a rapidly shrinking ice season in the Eeyou Marine Region. Perhaps the bears hunt seals from shorelines, adapting their predation techniques to bypass the need for ice floes. Local land users have observed bears stalking Canada geese, plundering bird nests for eggs, harvesting beavers, swimming after caribou, and scavenging beluga whale carcasses.

Later, I put the idea that polar bears could adapt to a land-based existence to Gregory Thiemann, professor of Arctic ecology at York University in Toronto and member of the IUCN Polar Bear Specialist Group. He was quick to offer a sharp reality check. “Polar bears need sea ice,” he said. “In the absence of sea ice, there are no polar bears. And the evidence for that is the fact that where there’s sea ice, there’s polar bears, and where there’s no sea ice, there’s no polar bears.”

**ICY PUZZLE:** Despite rapidly shrinking ice seasons, local people in James Bay have spotted healthy bears and cubs on rocky shores. _Credit: Sanford Diamond_

Genetically, polar bears (_Ursus maritimus_) split from brown bears (_Ursus arctos_) relatively recently in evolutionary history, remaining close enough to interbreed and produce fertile hybrids, Thiemann explained. But ecologically, they are entirely distinct. While brown bears thrive on land, polar bears are marine mammals whose entire physiology, fat storage, and hunting strategy evolved around sea ice.

Thiemann cautioned against mistaking opportunistic foraging for long-term population adaptation. He is not surprised by reports from Cree community members that bears have been seen hunting on land.

“Polar bears will eat everything they can because they’re bears,” Thiemann said. “They’ll eat beavers, snow goose eggs, garbage, and Ski-Doo seats. But none of these terrestrial foods can sustain a population of polar bears—full stop.” If land-based calories could support a 1,000-pound marine carnivore, Thiemann argued, an ecological niche would exist for large coastal brown bears along Hudson Bay. But where brown bears overlap with tundra habitat, they are small and scrawny, scraping by on ground squirrels and roots.

In the scientific literature, roughly 180 days a year without sea ice is widely recognized as the critical biological threshold beyond which adult polar bear survival drops sharply. However, the exact limit depends on sex, age, body condition, and reproductive status, Thiemann said. Individual bears vary widely in their hunting habits and tolerance to sea ice loss.

In the Eeyou Marine Region, polar bears are surviving right up against that theoretical limit. While seasonal ice cover varies widely from year to year, multiple years since the start of the century have recorded 175 to 180 ice-free days in the year. The growing fear is that current observations of healthy bears in James Bay are just a temporary anomaly, a reprieve in time, before inevitable further erosion of the regional population. “We will see a range contraction, and we will lose bears,” Thiemann said.

But the polar bears in the Eeyou Marine Region are not the only quirky population that appears to defy climate-based survival projections. In 2022, a study from southeastern Greenland documented an isolated enclave of polar bears—roughly numbering 200 animals—that bypassed the use of seasonal sea ice altogether. Their habitat currently experiences an annual ice-free period that exceeds the estimated fasting threshold for the species by more than 100 days. Researchers established that rather than forage on sea ice, the bears survive by hunting seals year-round at the terminus of glaciers.

**FUR TRAPPER:**Cree trapper Harry Erless tightens barbed wire onto a post. The wire snags a polar bear’s fur, from which DNA is analyzed. _Credit: Elena Kazamia_

Despite the rapidly warming climate, Thiemann thinks it is too early to be fatalistic about the fate of polar bears in the Eeyou Marine Region. “The outlook certainly isn’t positive right now, but that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t do everything we can to help conserve them,” he said.

Langwieder is hopeful given her preliminary analyses of diet based on the snagged hair. “I have the raw data, and it does seem that the bears are feeding from the marine system rather than the terrestrial system,” she told me. She is preparing to submit the results for publication. If accurate, her work would support observations by the Cree community that bears are successfully foraging seals despite loss of sea ice, demonstrating resilience and adaptation.

Thiemann believes there is great value in the partnership between Langwieder’s team at McGill University, the Eeyou Marine Wildlife Board, and the Cree Trappers Association. “The project will likely have important implications for human-polar bear coexistence,” Thiemann told me. “If changing habitat conditions increase nutritional stress on bears, they may be more likely to come into coastal communities looking for food. If you know where, when, and what bears are eating, you may be better able to predict and mitigate conflict and benefit conservation.” This is precisely the sentiment of the Cree trappers. “The last bear we killed was in 2018. We didn’t like doing it,” Sanford Diamond told me.

Whatever lies ahead for the polar bears of the Eeyou Marine Region, the partnership between Cree trappers and scientists stands as a vital success. It offers something increasingly rare: a practical, ground-level framework for weaving distinct ways of knowing into modern conservation.

**BELUGA MEAL:** Cree trapper Bernard Diamond shows off a beluga whale skull. Polar bears have been known to feed on beluga carcasses. _Credit: Elena Kazamia_

On our final stop, with the sun setting in a blaze of fire against the horizon, Erless recalled to me a similar evening in 2018, not too far from where we were standing. He was out on his knees picking wild cranberries, accompanied only by his son’s dog, when he felt the sudden prickle of being watched.

“I looked around at the rocks,” Erless told me. “It’s hard to tell because the rocks are white, but then I saw his head pop up. A big polar bear, watching me from about 300 meters away.” Erless kept his rifle close, but neither man nor bear moved aggressively. “He didn’t bother me, so I didn’t bother him. I just kept picking my cranberries.” He lit another cigarette and added jokingly, “You know, he probably knows me by this thing”—and motioned to the smoke drifting up and away from his hand.![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Secrets Hiding in a Duck-Billed Dinosaur’s Beak
content:
Hadrosaurs might not be the most popular dinosaurs among children, but they were extremely popular with natural selection. These duck-billed dinosaurs were some of the most common types of herbivores living during the Cretaceous period, and as such, they’re well-represented in the fossil record. Remarkably, we’re still learning new things about them and their eponymous bills.

For more than a decade, paleontologists puzzled over a series of bony projections around the front rim of the upper jaw of _Tethyshadros_, a genus of duck-billed dinosaur first discovered in Italy’s Villaggio del Pescatore. At first, they were believed to be a set of comb-like teeth, but now a new analysis [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1098/rsos.260392) in _Royal Society Open Science_ is revealing that they were far more complicated.

**Read more: “**[**This Bizarre Jurassic “Squid” Swam the Ancient Seas of Wyoming**](https://nautil.us/this-bizarre-jurassic-squid-swam-the-ancient-seas-of-wyoming-1286238)**”**

An international team of paleontologists conducted extensive micro-CT scans of the upper and lower jaw from a specimen named “Antonio,” the holotype of the genus. They determined that the mysterious spikes weren’t teeth at all—they weren’t even visible from the outside. Instead, they were a kind of scaffold supporting the dinosaur’s beak.

Made out of keratin (the same substance as fingernails), the beak had a complex network of minuscule bony channels feeding into it which housed nerves and capillaries. “What looked like a bizarre toothed or spiked beak may actually be the bony footprint of a much more complex living organ,” study author Marco Muscioni of the University of Bologna explained in a statement.

According to the team, it’s likely _Tethyshadros’_ beak functioned as a Swiss Army knife of sorts. A network of nerves wired it as a useful sensory organ for foraging, blood vessels indicate it could have helped radiate heat from its brain, and it was still sturdy enough to withstand the wear and tear grazing on gritty vegetation (in fact, it bears some resemblance to a cow’s hoof).

​​“Tethyshadros continues to surprise us,” study author Federico Fanti of the University of Bologna said. “The Villaggio del Pescatore fossils are among the most complete dinosaurs ever found in Europe, but new technologies are showing that even specimens we have studied for years can still preserve completely unexpected information.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Is This the Hidden Cause of Allergies?
content:
Allergies are on the rise. According to government statistics, cases of eczema, hay fever, and food allergies have been steadily climbing in the United States over the past few decades, leaving researchers puzzled. A slew of hypotheses for the increase have been offered—from too much hygiene to not enough gut microbes. Now, a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/all.70532) in the journal _Allergy_ suggests our understanding of the illnesses may be flawed from the beginning.

Allergies have traditionally been understood as an exaggerated response from an oversensitive immune system. A harmless allergen triggers a cascade of immune activity causing sneezes, inflammation, and in extreme cases even death. On a tissue level, part of the damage done by allergies has been to epithelial barrier cells lining the gut, skin, airways, and more. But what if we have things backwards?

**Read more: “**[**The Perils of Early Springtime**](https://nautil.us/the-perils-of-early-springtime-1196807)**”**

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” study author Peter K. Smith said in a statement. “Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces.”

Smith and a team developed the hypothesis after analyzing public datasets from more than 110 case-control cohorts, which included over 3,700 allergy patients, focusing on the genes that were transcribed in barrier cells. They found that genes responsible for clearing damaged mitochondria in the cells were less active in those suffering from allergies.

According to the team, this mitochondrial failure may represent the first domino to fall, which means it could be the primary cause of many allergies. Under their model, a leaky barrier stemming from dysfunctional mitochondria kickstarts the rest of the immune cascade, rather than vice versa. “The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so it raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow,” Smith explained.

The strongest evidence for the theory was among eosinophilic esophagitis patients, with all cohorts studied showing diminished mitochondria-clearing transcription activity. The same pattern was present in eczema patients—even among skin cells that weren’t inflamed. However, there were still some inconsistencies. Those with hay fever only showed a partially diminished capacity to clear damaged mitochondria, and the pattern was completely absent from those with asthma and nasal polyps.

In other words, there’s more work to be done. But the findings may give researchers a new perspective into a set of diseases that have been stubbornly rising. Or as Smith put it, “This is not a cure but is something we have never had before—a logical starting point.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: You Can Be Too Bored to Sleep
content:
Boredom is more interesting than you might think. For example, it comes in a few different flavors, like state boredom, or the feeling of wanting to engage in a stimulating activity but being unable to do so. Some people are also just more prone to experiencing boredom (contrary to popular parental maxims, these aren’t necessarily “boring people”). Now, a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2026.114110) in the journal _Personality and Individual Differences_ finds a relationship between boredom and sleep.

Previous research has shown that chronic boredom is linked to difficulties with self-control. “For most people, boredom can serve as a call to action,” study author James Danckert explained in a [statement](https://uwaterloo.ca/news/arts/research/boredom-closely-related-poor-sleep). “But for people who suffer from chronic boredom, it’s very difficult to take action and can have a range of negative outcomes, from higher rates of depression and anxiety to increased drug and alcohol use, problem gambling, and problematic smartphone use.”

**Read more: “**[**What Boredom Does to You**](https://nautil.us/what-boredom-does-to-you-236854)**”**

So Danckert and a team of his fellow psychologists from the University of Waterloo recruited two groups of undergraduates to complete a series of questionnaires recording their boredom proneness, sleep quality, and bedtime procrastination. Additionally, the team measured one group’s sleep hygiene, state boredom, and rumination (persistent negative thinking). Both groups also underwent assessments of their self-control, depression, and anxiety.

After controlling for a variety of variables, the team found that proneness to boredom was associated with poorer sleep quality. Bedtime procrastination was a little less consistent—one group showed a link between boredom proneness and delaying turning in for the night, but the other didn’t. Finally, rumination showed a closer association with momentary state boredom than proneness to boredom overall.

What does it all mean?

According to the team, it’s likely that end-of-day fatigue makes it more difficult for the boredom prone to get started on their bedtime routines. FOMO, late-night phone use, and a general preference for instant gratification could conspire to keep the boredom prone from getting some much-needed shut-eye.

Relatedly, improving bedtime routines could offer some relief to the boredom prone. “Focusing on improving sleep hygiene likely represents a fruitful avenue for helping the highly boredom prone deal more effectively with the negatively valenced experience of boredom,” the researchers wrote.

Something to remember the next time you find yourself doomscrolling into the wee hours. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Bees Make Better Dads Than We Thought
content:
What are male bumblebees even for?

Queen bees control the fertilization of their eggs with diploid females becoming workers who gather food and the cheaper-to-produce haploid males becoming drones. Traditionally, these males were thought to only contribute the genetic material necessary to kickstart a new colony, earning them the dismissive nickname “flying sperm bags.” But now a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1098/rsos.261826) in _Royal Society Open Science_ suggests they may be much more important.

Prior to this study, just one other [investigation](https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.82.19.6371) (by Sydney Cameron, now at the University of Illinois), probed the role males play in bumblebee colonies and found they shared in the brood care of their siblings. It piqued the curiosity of a team of entomologists from the University of California, Riverside, so they snapped some thermal photos of bumblebee nests. The images showed males poised over the brood in an “incubation posture.” This allows them to make contact with eggs while they work their muscles, generating heat.

“I was quite surprised to see them incubating,” study author Meghan Moore said in a [statement](https://news.ucr.edu/articles/2026/11/19/boy-bumblebees-are-more-flying-sperm-sacs). “In the literature, they say the males’ only purpose is to be ‘flying bags of sperm,’ that their only purpose is to mate with queens. But our research, and Sydney’s, shows this just isn’t true.”

To investigate further, the team set up some artificial bumblebee colonies back in the lab. Each colony started with an already mated queen (as they do in the wild). To these the team added either one, three, five, or zero additional male bumblebees. Then they watched, for roughly a month, occasionally peeking inside with thermal cameras.

They found that the males who went into incubation mode had hotter thoraxes (by as much as seven degrees Fahrenheit). Curiously, their incubation temp was still lower than the average queen’s, which the researchers think might be to protect their sperm cells.

They also discovered that the presence of males ramped up bee production. “Queens with males in their nests began laying eggs twice as fast, and they end up with up to 1.5 times more brood,” Moore said. “This is an important result at a time when bumblebee populations are threatened by pollution and habitat loss.”

There were a couple of caveats, however. In the wild, colonies start as a women’s only club, with queens and workers and no males. Additionally, the males in the lab-created colonies were prevented from leaving, which they tend to do under natural conditions.

“It is possible these males helped as much as they did because there weren’t female workers in the nests we created for this study,” Moore explained. “Though we don’t think lack of females caused what we saw. In a smaller study we observed males doing some caring even in the presence of female workers.”

In other words, we can probably stop calling them “flying bags of sperm.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Can Psychedelics Improve Decision-making?
content:
In 1972, Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Dock Ellis pitched a no-hitter against the San Diego Padres. It’s an impressive feat on its own, but Ellis, under the mistaken assumption he had the day off, had taken a couple hits of LSD before the game. Completely zonked on acid, he managed to last through nine scoreless innings, leading his team to a 2-0 victory. Is it possible the drugs helped? Well, a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeb3041) in _Science Advances_ suggests psychedelics could lead to better decision-making (at least in mice).

To investigate the link between psychedelic drugs and decision-making, a team of Boston University neuroscientists put laboratory mice through a simple test. The lab animals were offered three holes, poking their noses through the center one kicked the experiment off. The other two holes had blinking lights that flashed either quickly or slowly, a nose poke in the fast-flashing hole earned the rodents a sugary reward.

**Read more: “**[**The Promise and Peril of Toad Smoking, the Everest of Psychedelics**](https://nautil.us/the-promise-and-peril-of-toad-smoking-the-everest-of-psychedelics-1284999)**”**

Of course, the mice weren’t privy to the experimental design, so they had to learn which sensory cues led to the reward. Untreated mice made some mistakes. Some tended to favor either the right or left side, regardless of the flashing, for example. Mice that were dosed with psychedelics—either psilocybin or ketamine—were more accurate. Other drugs, like cocaine and diazepam, didn’t show the same effects.

According to the team, the psychedelic drug treatments may have freed the mice from their prior biases. “These findings reveal how psychedelics reduce the reliance on habits and repetitive choices, which may explain part of their therapeutic effect,” study author Benjamin Scott explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1152304).

It’s a finding that harmonizes with a model called [REBUS](https://nautil.us/psychedelics-open-a-new-window-on-the-mechanisms-of-perception-238244) (RElaxed Beliefs Under pSychedelics). Under this model, psychedelics make our brains a bit more cognitively supple and open. In this case, they may have made the mice learn the sensory cues more quickly.

“Both drugs strengthen the influence of sensory evidence on choices and reduce the effect of bias,” Scott explained. “Thus, decisions became more accurate, guided by the immediate sensory environment of the animals and less influenced by other factors, like the bias to repeat the same choice over again.”

The team did uncover a potential trade-off, however. Although their choices were more accurate, the dosed mice took a bit longer to decide. “Extrapolating on this, you could imagine that in situations where processing speed or reaction time is critical, for example, while driving or playing sports, these drugs could negatively affect performance,” Scott said.

That may explain why Dock Ellis went 0 for 3 at the plate that fateful day. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
